# High spin superatom stabilized by dual subshell filling

Dinesh Bista1,‡, Alexander P. Aydt2,‡, Kevin J. Anderton3, Daniel W. Paley2, Theodore A. Betley3, Arthur C. Reber1, Vikas Chauhan4, Amymarie K. Bartholomew2,*, Xavier Roy2,*, and Shiv N. Khanna1,*

1 Department of Physics, Virginia Commonwealth University, Richmond, VA 23220, USA

2 Department of Chemistry, Columbia University, New York, NY 10027, USA

3 Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA

4 Ramjas College, University of Delhi, Delhi-110007, India

‡ These authors contributed equally.

ABSTRACT: Quantum confinement in small symmetric clusters leads to the bunching of electronic states into closely packed shells, enabling the classification of clusters with well-defined valences as superatoms. Like atoms, superatomic clusters with filled shells exhibit enhanced electronic stability. Here we show that octahedral transition metal chalcogenide clusters can achieve filled shell electronic configurations when they have 100 valence electrons in 50 orbitals or 114 valence electrons in 57 orbitals. While these stable clusters are intrinsically diamagnetic, we use our understanding of their electronic structures to theoretically predict that a cluster with 107 valence electrons would uniquely combine high stability and high spin magnetic moment, attained by filling a majority subshell of 57 electrons and a minority subshell of 50 electrons. We experimentally demonstrate this predicted stability, high spin magnetic moment (S = 7∕2), and fully delocalized electronic structure in the new cluster [NEt4]5[Fe6S8(CN)6]. This work presents the first computational and experimental demonstration of the importance of dual subshell filling in transition metal chalcogenide clusters.

Quantum confinement in small symmetric clusters leads to the grouping of electronic states into shells. For clusters where valence electrons completely fill these shells, an unusually large energy gap between the Highest Occupied Molecular Orbital (HOMO) and Lowest Unoccupied Molecular Orbital (LUMO) occurs.1-4 When the properties of the clusters are dominated by the enhancement in stability gained by closing their electronic shells, the clusters may be classified as superatoms.5-10 For metallic clusters, the electron counts leading to filled shells have been rationalized based on a confined nearly free electrons gas.1

Transition metal chalcogenide clusters are an attractive class of building blocks for assembling solid state materials.11-

13 One of the most common such clusters is the octahedral metal chalcogenide TM6E8L6 (see structures in Figure 1), where TM = transition metal; E = chalcogen; L = ligand. Prepared in solutions or in the solid state, these clusters can be highly stable, have charge donor/acceptor characteristics, and can form multicomponent solids with complementary units while maintaining their internal structures.14-21 Functional solids made using these building blocks offer programmable properties, including tunable and switchable magnetic ordering, electrical conductivity, optical properties, and thermal transport.11, 22-26 One of the key advantages over traditional atomic solids is that the electronic and magnetic characteristics of the individual building blocks can be programmed preassembly, offering unique levels of control over the properties

of the assembled materials.27-32 Octahedral Fe6 clusters synthesized in the Betley group on a templating ligand scaffold have even been shown to achieve giant spin ground states up to S = 19/2 with electronic structures characteristic of superatoms.33-36

The electron count of octahedral TM6E8L6 is calculated by adding the valence electrons of each TM atom, six electrons for each chalcogen atom, and two electrons for each ligand. These clusters have high symmetry, producing significant degeneracy in their electronic structures that confer high electronic stability to certain electron counts. Take Co6E8L6 and [Re6E8L6]2+, two of the most ubiquitous clusters in the literature,37-38 as illustrative examples: Co6E8L6 has 114 electrons distributed in 57 orbitals, and [Re6E8L6]2+ has 100 electrons distributed in 50 orbitals. While both electron counts lead to remarkably stable cores due to their closed shells, it also produces diamagnetic clusters, which limits their utility. The realization of clusters with high magnetic moments is important for many applications, including in single-molecule magnets,39-41 magnetic superatomic crystals and catalysts.42-44 In this work, we explore the electronic structures of octahedral TM6E8L6 clusters and provide a new understanding for their stability and magnetic properties based on electron counting rules and dual subshell filling.45-48

We theoretically and experimentally investigate the inorganic core Fe6S8 and find that it is most stable in the 1+ oxidation state with a spin magnetic moment of 7 μb and with the filled majority and minority subshells having electron counts

## 2

of 57 and 50. We synthesize the novel cluster [Fe6S8(CN)6]5– (1+ core, giving 107 electrons) using electron-accepting cyanide ligands to stabilize the high charge state.49-53 Our reason for focusing on this novel cluster instead of the previously reported [Fe6S8(PEt3)6]+ cluster is that cyanides can be used as bridging ligands capable of mediating strong magnetic ex-

change, for example in Prussian Blue-type materials.54-55 Consistent with our theoretical predictions, we experimentally find the cluster [Fe6S8(CN)6]5– is stable and has an isolated magnetic spin state of S = 7∕2. In the solid state, the magnetic moment is smaller than expected, suggesting antiferromagnetic intercluster interactions. This is supported by calculations of the magnetic configuration of the solid state structure indicating that the antiferromagnetic arrangement is lowest in energy. On the whole, the dual subshell filling of [Fe6S8(CN)6]5– produces a magnetic superatom that combines a well-defined valence, a large HOMO-LUMO gap and a high spin state.25, 42, 56-57

A dual subshell filling is a concept that explains the formation of a stable cluster with a high spin magnetic moment. A dual subshell filling is when a cluster is stabilized in its spin up channel via one magic number, and the cluster’s spin down channel is filled with a different magic number. This leads to a cluster with a larger HOMO-LUMO gap, a spin magnetic moment, and a hybrid electronic structure (Figure 1). We first

model the prototypical diamagnetic closed shell clusters Co6E8L6 and [Re6E8L6]2+ as Co6S8(CO)6 and [Re6S8(CO)6]2+ (Figure 1; details are in Supplementary Figure 11). Co6S8(CO)6 has an electron count of 114 valence electrons (6×9 electrons derived from Co, 8×6 electrons from S, and 6×2 electrons in the Co–CO bonds), and a large HOMO–LUMO gap of 1.71 eV. Note that this valence electron count does not include the electrons within the ligand itself. [Re6E8(CO)6]2+, on the other hand, has an electron count of 100 and a HOMO–LUMO gap of 1.88 eV. When compared to [Re6E8(CO)6]2+, the additional 14 electrons of Co6S8(CO)6 occupy A2g, T1g, and T2u orbitals; these close-lying sets of high symmetry orbitals are the reason why certain electron counts are favored.

To design an electronically stable dual subshell magnetic cluster from the Co6S8(CO)6 and [Re6S8(CO)6]2+ orbital configurations, we derive the spin up channel from the larger closed shell structure (Co6S8(CO)6) and the spin down channel from the smaller one ([Re6S8(CO)6]2+). The cluster [Fe6S8(CN)6]5– has an ideal electron count of 107 electrons to realize this concept (Figure 1). In [Fe6S8(CN)6]5–, the majorityfilled subshell consists of orbitals corresponding to the 114 electron configuration (spin up channel), with 57 electrons before a large energy gap. The minority subshell configuration (spin down channel) consists of orbitals derived from the 100 electron configuration, with 50 electrons below its energy gap. The result is a cluster with a sizeable HOMO-LUMO gap and a large spin magnetic moment resulting from 7 excess (unpaired) electrons in the majority spin channel (shown in red in Figure 1).

To probe the stability of [Fe6S8(CN)6]5–, we computationally assemble the cluster stepwise, starting from the naked neutral core Fe6S8. Without ligand, the inorganic core adopts a C4v symmetry, and has a spin magnetic moment of 8 µB in which four equivalent equatorial Fe atoms have local spin magnetic moments of 1.6 µB, and the apical Fe atoms have local spin moments of 2.1 µB and 0.4 µB (Supplementary Figure 4). The symmetry-breaking distortion can be visualized as the low spin Fe moving towards the core and the high spin Fe moving away from the core. Next, we sequentially add neutral cyanide ligands (CN) to Fe6S8, which reduces the net spin magnetic moment to 7, 0, 3, 0, 1 and 0 µB for Fe6S8(CN)m with m = 1 – 6 (Figure 2a and Supplementary Figure 4). For m = 2, 4, and 6, the local Fe moments are not quenched, but the symmetric placement of CN produces an antiferromagnetic configuration and zero net magnetic moment.

We then sequentially add electrons and accompanying charge-balancing tetraethylammonium (NEt4) cations to Fe6S8(CN)6, and examine how the HOMO-LUMO gap and spin magnetic moment of [NEt4]n[Fe6S8(CN)6] changes with the charge state (n) (Figure 2b). For n = 1 – 4 and 6, the HOMO-LUMO gap is relatively small (≲ 0.4 eV). The 107 electron cluster [NEt4]5[Fe6S8(CN)6] has the largest HOMO- LUMO gap of the series (0.82 eV), indicating that the 5– charge state has a particularly stable electronic configuration. This maximum in the HOMO-LUMO gap also coincides with the highest spin magnetic moment, as expected for a cluster with a filled dual subshell.

A detailed analysis of the one-electron energy levels of [NEt4]5[Fe6S8(CN)6] elucidates the origins of its electronic stability and high spin magnetic moment (Figure 2c). By analogy to the formation of shells in atoms, our calculations show that in the [Fe6S8(CN)6]n– system, electronic states bunch into shells which are separated by large energy gaps. The complete

## 3

filling of these grouped electronic states yields closed electronic shell configurations, conferring high stability to the cluster. A key feature revealed by the one-electron energy levels diagram of [NEt4]5[Fe6S8(CN)6] is the large exchange splitting energy between the occupied states in the spin up channel and their corresponding unoccupied states in the spin down channel (color coded in Figure 2c). The average exchange splitting energy is 1.24 eV, and we show the exchange splitting of two representative examples out of the seven pairs of half-filled orbitals. The exchange splitting energy between the LUMO in the spin down channel and its corresponding occupied orbital in thespin up channel is 1.61 eV while that between the HOMO in thespin up channel and its corresponding unoccupied orbital in the spin down channel is 0.99 eV. Supplementary Figure 10 shows all seven exchange splitting energies. As a result of this large exchange splitting, the electronic structure of [NEt4]5[Fe6S8(CN)6] is fully spin polarized with HOMO-LUMO gaps of 1.57 and 0.86 eV in the majority and minority spin channels, respectively.

The spin-polarized electronic structure of [NEt4]n[Fe6S8(CN)6] suggests that the filling of the one-electron states will not follow the simple S = 0, ½, 0, ½, … pattern, and could instead produce large magnetic moments for certain electron counts. Starting from the neutral S = 0 cluster Fe6S8(CN)6, which has a total number of 6 unfilled states in the majority and minority channels, the fundamental question is whether one can stabilize a ferromagnetic ground state

by filling both the spin up and spin down manifolds, in analogy to Hund’s rule in atoms. Figure 2b shows the spin magnetic moment of [NEt4]n[Fe6S8(CN)6] as a function of the number of electrons added to the cluster (i.e. as function of n). The spin magnetic moment of each individual Fe atom for all cluster charge states is displayed in Supplementary Figure 9. For clusters with low electron counts (n = 0 – 3), the ferrimagnetic and antiferromagnetic states are close in energy, and the magnetic moment cannot be predicted a priori using a simple electron filling analogy. By contrast, highly charged clusters (n = 4 – 6) have ferromagnetic ground states and thus large spin magnetic moments, with a maximum moment of 7 μB attained in [NEt4]5[Fe6S8(CN)6]. Both [NEt4]4[Fe6S8(CN)6] and [NEt4]6[Fe6S8(CN)6] have smaller moments of 6 μB, implying that the first five electrons added to the core occupy states in the spin up channel to fill the subshell, while the sixth electron goes in the LUMO of the spin down channel, thereby reducing the magnetic moment by 1 µB. This is analogous to Hund’s rule, but for clusters.

To summarize, these calculations show that the dual subshell electronic structure of [NEt4]5[Fe6S8(CN)6] produces a closed electronic shell configuration in both spin channels, and a large spin magnetic moment. The excess electrons in the spin up channel are ferromagnetically aligned, producing a net magnetic moment of 7 μB. This configuration is highly dependent on the electron count, such that the removal or addition of one electron leads to a change of 1 μB in the spin mag-

netic moment. However, on removal of two electrons, the predictions of the spin magnetic moment based on the electron count become inaccurate as antiferromagnetic coupling settles in. Computationally, the stability of the S = 7∕2 spin configuration appears general for isoelectronic clusters such as [Fe6S8(CO)6]+ (Supplementary Figure 12). Furthermore, [Fe6S8(PR3)6]+ has been experimentally reported in different charge states and indeed, the monocationic [Fe6S8(PR3)6]+ is the most stable charge state, with an effective magnetic moment corresponding to a spin state of S = 7∕2.58

A simplistic approach to predict the stability of clusters a priori is to consider the most stable oxidation states of the constituent transition metal sites. In particular, Fe is more stable as Fe(III) than as Fe(II). In [Fe6S8(CN)6]4–, all six metal sites would be formally Fe(III), yet this 4– charge state is not particularly electronically stable, especially compared to the 5– cluster. This suggests that the electronic structure of these clusters is best understood by considering the collective electronic states of the cluster orbitals, and not the properties of the individual atoms within the cluster core. Hence, viewing the cluster as a superatom with an unusual electronic configuration that seeks to maximize its spin state is the most fruitful way of understanding its properties.

Having computationally determined the stability and magnetic properties of [NEt4]5[Fe6S8(CN)6], we sought to experimentally confirm these predictions. The title compound is prepared by treating [Fe6S8(PEt3)6][BF4]2 with excess [NEt4][CN] in acetonitrile at room temperature.59 [NEt4]5[Fe6S8(CN)6] crystallizes from the solution as black needles after 6 hours. Note that the [Fe6S8]2+ core of the starting material is spontaneously reduced under the reaction conditions to yield [NEt4]5[Fe6S8(CN)6] (rather than [NEt4]4[Fe6S8(CN)6]), which is consistent with the predicted increased stability of the 107 electron cluster.

Single crystals of [NEt4]5[Fe6S8(CN)6] (structure shown in Fig. 3a) form in the C2/c space group with an asymmetric unit containing 3 distinct Fe positions and the other three Fe sites generated by symmetry. The cluster has a nearly Oh structure with an average Fe…Fe distance of 2.63 Å and a standard deviation of 0.01 Å. Computationally, [NEt4]5[Fe6S8(CN)6] is found to have D4h symmetry (Figure 2a), although the energy difference between this structure and the Oh one is only 0.11 eV, and the difference in spin magnetic moment is negligible.

The cyclic voltammogram of [NEt4]5[Fe6S8(CN)6] (Figure 3b) features reversible redox events for both the reduction of the 5− cluster to the 6− cluster occurring at −1.06 V relative to the ferrocene/ferrocenium redox couple (Fc/Fc+), and the oxidation of the 5− cluster to the 4− cluster at −0.21 V vs. Fc/Fc+. In mixed valent systems such as this, it is possible to quantify the degree of delocalization by the spacing between the redox events.60-62 The comproportionation constant KC represents the ratio between the mixed valent ([NEt4]5[Fe6S8(CN)6] represented as 5−) and isovalent states ([NEt4]4[Fe6S8(CN)6] and [NEt4]6[Fe6S8(CN)6] represented as 4− and 6−, respectively), and may be calculated electrochemically based on the Nernst equation:

The comproportionation constant of 2.06×1014 calculated for [NEt4]5[Fe6S8(CN)6] indicates complete electron delocalization within the cluster core (Robin-Day class III). For reference, Robin-Day class I materials (fully localized) typically have KC < 102, class II (intermediate valency) have 102 < KC < 106, and class III (fully delocalized) have KC > 106.63-64 Consistent with a fully delocalized system, the 57Fe Mӧssbauer spectrum (Fig. 3c) of [NEt4]5[Fe6S8(CN)6] taken at 210 K shows only one quadrupole doublet (δ = 0.26 mm/s,│ΔEQ│ = 0.67 mm/s). The extent of delocalization supports our theoretical conclusions that the electronic structure of the cluster is best understood as a collective whole rather than in terms of individual Fe sites. Note that the isomer shift and the presence of only one quadrupole doublet in [NEt4]5[Fe6S8(CN)6] is consistent with the 57Fe Mӧssbauer spectrum of isoelectronic [Fe6S8(PEt3)6]+, which is also understood to be a fully delocalized mixed-valence system.65

creases monotonically with increasing temperature, indicating that the cluster does not follow a simple Curie-Weiss law. Between 50 and 250 K, 𝜇𝑒𝑓𝑓 increases from 5.9 to 7. These values are lower than the expected value for a S = 7∕2 cluster (𝜇𝑒𝑓𝑓 = 7.9). By contrast, 𝜇𝑒𝑓𝑓 of [NEt4]5[Fe6S8(CN)6] measured in a deuterated methanol solution using the NMR-based Evans method is temperature independent between 200 and 300 K, indicating a well-isolated spin state, and the experimental value (𝜇𝑒𝑓𝑓 ~8) agrees well with the predicted one. The difference between the solid state and solution state 𝜇𝑒𝑓𝑓 strongly suggests that intercluster magnetic interactions in the solid state lower the magnetic moment of the sample. In solution, the clusters are on average far apart and the intercluster magnetic interactions are negligible. The Evans method thus provides a more direct probe of the intrinsic spin magnetic moment of the cluster, which agrees very well with the dual subshell electronic structure model.

Calculations on the unit cell of [NEt4]5[Fe6S8(CN)6] obtained from single crystal X-ray diffraction support our hypothesis that intercluster magnetic interactions in the solid state lower the measured spin magnetic moment (the energyoptimized structure is shown in Figure 4b). The cluster centroids are separated by ~1 nm, and the model indicates that the antiferromagnetic state is lowest in energy, followed closely by the ferrimagnetic and the ferromagnetic states. Each unit cell has four [Fe6S8(CN)6]5− clusters, and the relative energy of the cluster-assembled material with different spin magnetic moments is shown in Figure 4c. Comprising two spin-up clusters (7 μB) and two spin-down clusters (−7 μB), the antiferromagnetic configuration with a total spin magnetic moment of 0 μB is the lowest energy state. The 14 μB ferrimagnetic configuration with three spin-up and one spin-down clusters is only 4 meV higher in energy. In comparison, the 28 μB ferromagnetic configuration is 28 meV higher in energy than the antiferromagnetic configuration. All other configurations are at least 0.4 eV higher in energy than those made of clusters with local spin magnetic moments of 7 μB or −7 μB, yet again indicating that there is strong energetic preference for the 7 μB electronic structure of the cluster. The energies of the competing magnetic configurations show that the magnetic interactions between the clusters are weak and favor antiferromagnetic and ferrimagnetic configurations, which lower the measured magnetic moment below the expected value of 7 μB per cluster. This effect is more pronounced at

low temperature and gradually subsides with increasing temperature as the ferromagnetic state becomes more populated.

In this work, we have introduced a new strategy to design magnetic superatoms. Using [Fe6S8(CN)6]5– as a model system, we have shown that the dual subshell filling model produces a remarkably stable electronic structure with a well-defined valence and a high magnetic moment of 7 μB due to the spin majority and spin minority channels both having the optimal number of electrons to create a large HOMO–LUMO gap. These predictions are broadly realized experimentally in the newly synthesized cluster [NEt4]5[Fe6S8(CN)6]. The fact that its electronic properties are dominated by the stability it achieves with an electron count of 107 establishes [Fe6S8(CN)6]5– as a unique magnetic superatom. Furthermore, the cyanide ligands open the door to the design of extended structures with long range magnetic order assembled from magnetic superatoms.
